To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the Alpine Fault dips ∼75°–80°E, (b) it has ∼35 m of vertical offset of a late Pleistocene erosion surface, and (c) it is associated with a zone of deformation in the hanging wall that is ∼100 m wide and ∼100 m thick.
the Alpine Fault, an active continental transform that is capable of generating damaging earthquakes, has an average dip of 80°, and there is a significant normal drag component on the fault.
we have acquired and processed a 360 m ultrahigh‐resolution reflection profile across the central section of the Alpine Fault in South Westland, New Zealand.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of ultrahigh‐resolution imaging techniques and the application of these methods to the Alpine Fault.

the structural evolution of a major active fault zone and demonstrates the utility of ultrashallow seismic reflection profiling for the detailed imaging of active fault zones and the determination of slip rates.

the development of a new technique that can be used to image active faults and their shallow structures, which is important to the assessment of seismic hazard and to the understanding of the mechanics of faulting.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the Alpine Fault is a major active continental strike-slip fault with reverse-slip components, that the fault is capable of generating major earthquakes, and that the fault has a significant dip-slip component.
the Alpine Fault is a reverse-slip fault, with a component of dextral slip.
our data are consistent with the Alpine Fault accommodating ∼2 mm/yr of reverse slip and ∼10 mm/yr of dextral slip.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the seismic data provide a new, high-resolution image of a major active continental fault zone, and the images are consistent with previous interpretations based on other geophysical and geologic methods.
we have imaged the Alpine Fault zone and surrounding structures to a depth of 150 m with a vertical resolution of <0.2 m, and we have obtained a preliminary slip rate for the Alpine Fault.

we are able to image the Alpine Fault and its shallow deformation structures with high resolution and that our data are consistent with the fault zone geometry and deformational processes proposed by previous studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Alpine Fault is a complex structure, and the fault zone is a highly heterogeneous region that is capable of producing a variety of ground motions and surface ruptures during earthquakes.
ultrahigh-resolution shallow seismic imaging of active faults can yield high-resolution structural information that is complementary to other geophysical and geological methods.
ultrahigh-resolution reflection imaging is capable of providing high-resolution structural data that are critical for assessing the seismic hazard of active faults.
